Xuan Kong Flying Star — orientation, annotation, site model, worksheet

Review material · bundle com.shenxuankong.app · 1.0.0 (10) · English interface

This page follows the app in the order it is actually used: first why anyone needs it, then step by step to the printed worksheet. The seventeen operation screenshots are all taken from the build under review, by clicking through the app in a simulator — the facing was typed in and confirmed, the indoor cells were marked by tapping palaces, the outdoor objects were chosen from the marking sheet, and the ruler was raised by tapping an object on the model. None of them is a mock-up. Three sample pages of the worksheet are the app’s own export.

1. Why a user needs this

Someone who takes on a flat, a shop unit or an office has only a few things to establish first: which way this place faces, which of the 24 mountains that measured facing falls on, where the air comes in, what needs to be blocked, and what needs to be opened up. None of that is a vague judgement — it lands on a direction, a number of metres, and a specific wall.

But on site there are only two things at hand: a tape measure and a phone. Most of what is on the phone stops at showing a compass — it gives a degree figure and that is the end of it. What happens after the degree (what this palace governs, which wall that building outside presses on, what to move and where to move it) is left to guesswork, or to hiring someone.

This app covers the part after the degree. It takes the facing as its first input, computes the chart from it, keeps an indoor and an outdoor ledger, builds a measured three-dimensional model of what is actually outside, gives a verdict and a handling for each marked object, and prints the result as a document a contractor can work from. Every rule behind those verdicts comes from a book transmitted from the Ming dynasty — Shen’s Xuan Kong Xue — not from our own extrapolation and not from generated text.

2. Step one is the facing: an input, not a readout

The app opens on the casting screen. The first screen does not give content; it gives an entry waiting to be filled — Pending, with one line saying a single reading at the door or a window is enough. The device magnetometer can be used on the spot, or a figure can be typed in from a physical compass, which some users prefer because they cannot hold a phone steady at the door.

Fig. 1 — It opens on the casting screen

No feed, no card of the day — just an entry waiting to be filled: Pending, with one line saying it only takes one reading at the door or a window. Below it, the venue type (home / shop / office). When the direction has not been taken, the app says so instead of pretending it knows.

The entry point is a measurement, not a piece of content.

Once the figure is entered and confirmed, the app returns the sitting and facing with its fenjin division: Sitting Chen · Facing Xu, sitting 120°, Ren-Chen middle fenjin. Everything downstream is built on that number: the nine-palace chart is laid out from it, the indoor palaces are divided by it, the outdoor model is oriented by it, and every verdict has to say which palace and which mountain it refers to. If the user measures wrong, everything after is wrong — the app will not guess a facing for them.

Fig. 2 — After setting it: Sitting Chen · Facing Xu, 120°

A degree figure is typed into the orientation block and confirmed, and the app returns Sitting Chen · Facing Xu, sitting 120°, Ren-Chen middle fenjin. That number then carries through everything: the nine-palace chart, the indoor ledger, the outdoor model and every verdict below it.

The facing is an input. The figure the user measured decides every output that follows.

Fig. 3 — The nine-palace chart

The chart only appears once the facing is set. Each palace is labelled with its position, its direction and the two stars that govern it, plus what that palace favours and what it does not. Before a facing is set, this block is empty — the app does not guess.

The output is geometry and arithmetic, not a paragraph generated at random.

3. One chart, three venue types

After the facing comes the question of what this place is for: home, business (a shop unit), or office. This is not a change of label. Each venue carries its own indoor ledger and its own wording: a home is read by door, bedrooms, stove and toilet; a shop by counter, stock area and entrance flow; an office by reception, workstations and meeting rooms. Same chart — not the same question.

Fig. 4 — One chart, three venue types

The same chart, but first: what is this place used for? Home / business / office. The venue decides what gets marked indoors and how the verdicts are worded. The same room, lived in or traded from, is not the same question.

The rule set switches with the venue — it is not a house with the labels renamed.

4. Indoors: marking what each palace is used for

Indoors is marked cell by cell. Tap a palace and the sheet rises: first the mountain level (Ren / Zi / Gui within Kan, for instance, or the whole palace), then what is in it — door, bedroom, living room, kitchen, bathroom, study — plus how much of that corner is missing. The mountain level matters because within this method two mountains of one palace are not interchangeable: doorways are read against the facing star, bed and stove against the mountain star, and the reading only lands correctly when the mountain is right.

Fig. 5 — Indoor ledger: every cell waits to be marked

Under each of the nine palaces sits + mark a function. Until it is marked, the app only says what that palace governs; it never decides on the user’s behalf that the main bedroom is in this one.

An empty cell stays empty — it is not filled in, and not guessed at.

Fig. 6 — Tap a palace, the marking sheet rises

Tap Kan (due north): the sheet offers the finer mountain level (Ren / Zi / Gui, or the whole palace), then the function grouped by kind (door, bedroom, living, kitchen, bathroom, study…), plus how much of the corner is missing. The mountain level matters because within this method two mountains of the same palace are not the same thing.

Annotation goes down to the 24-mountain level, not to “roughly this side”.

Once marked, that palace enters the computation with its label: what it governs, whether this use belongs there, and if not, which of the two should move. The ledger belongs to the user — for a cell they have not marked, the app only says what the palace governs; it never asserts that the main bedroom is in this one.

Fig. 7 — Marked: three rooms, three palaces

Kan is marked Master bedroom, Li is marked Living room and Zhen is marked Kitchen. From then on each palace’s reading, its missing-corner note and the matching line in the worksheet are computed from its own label. Change a label and the conclusions change with it.

The user marks it, the app computes it — the ledger is theirs, not ours.

Switching to office or business changes the whole ledger on the same page — reception, workstations and meeting rooms, or counter, stock and entrance flow. The verdicts change with it, because how people spend time in the place is different.

Fig. 8 — Switched to Office: same page, different vocabulary

Same chart, same nine palaces. The indoor ledger becomes a workplace: reception, workstations, meeting rooms — here Li carries Meeting room, and the verdict below reads that palace against it.

Switching venue really does switch the rule set.

Fig. 9 — Switched to Business: counter and foot traffic

The commercial ledger: storefront, checkout, stock, entrance flow — here Li carries Checkout. The same nine palaces, read as a place of business.

A shop is not a house with a few words swapped out.

5. Outdoors: marking what is actually out there

The outdoor ledger is kept separate and is never merged with the indoor one. That is not an interface choice; it is how the method works. Indoors is “how people use this space”; outdoors is “what outside is acting on this space”. Each has its own reading, and flattening them into one list mixes two different things.

Objects outside are placed onto the nine palaces by mountain. The sheet groups them by how they act rather than alphabetically: solid·blocking (trees, a neighbouring tower, hills, walls, boulders), void·conducting (roads, water, wells, malls, lifts), spanning (bridges), fire·pointed (towers, a neighbouring kitchen, poles, an opposite corner), plus missing corners. Anything not on the list can be typed in and is still classified.

Fig. 10 — Outdoor ledger: what is out there, marked on the eight sides

A separate ledger: things that physically exist outside are placed onto the nine palaces by mountain. It is never merged with the indoor ledger — one chart, two ledgers, each read on its own terms.

Two ledgers kept apart is how the method is actually practised.

Fig. 11 — Outdoor marking sheet: grouped by how it acts

Objects are not listed alphabetically. They are grouped by the way they act on the house: solid·blocking (trees, a neighbouring tower, hills, walls, boulders), void·conducting (roads, water, wells, malls, lifts), spanning (bridges), fire·pointed (towers, a neighbouring kitchen, poles, an opposite corner), plus missing corners. Anything not listed can be typed in and still gets classified.

Grouping by action is what lets the verdict land on “blocks / conducts / strikes”.

Fig. 12 — Marked: Zhen carries “Neighbouring tall block”

Choosing it drops that entry into Zhen (due east), and the page immediately reads that side: what this direction governs, which wall the object presses on, and whether anything needs doing about it.

Annotation and verdict are two steps of one chain, not two unrelated tables.

6. The sandbox: from annotation to a model you can measure

What was marked stands up in the sandbox. The blue-lit tower at the centre is your own home — 30 floors, with the blue band wrapping the floor you are on (F21, eye height 62 m; the gold dashed line is your eye level). The neighbouring tall block, the trees, the water and the tower each sit at their true bearing and stand at their true height, so which one is above you and which wall the qi strikes is visible at a glance. Red beams are the sha pressing on the house; teal arcs the qi arriving; the lit segment on the ground ring marks where it comes from. Drag to turn the view, tap an object to change its size.

Fig. 13 — The sandbox: what you marked, stood up in volumes

The four marked objects stand up as solids here: the neighbouring tall block in Zhen, the trees in Xun, the water in Kan, the tower in Qian. The blue-lit tower at the centre is your own home (30 floors); the blue band wraps your floor (F21, eye height 62 m — the gold dashed line is your eye level). Red beams are the sha pressing on the house, teal arcs the qi arriving, and the lit segment on the ground ring marks the direction it comes from. Drag to turn the view; tap an object to select it.

Every height, floor and bearing is a real measure from what the user marked — not a drawing.

7. Ruler and verdict: every conclusion hangs on a measurement

Tapping an object raises the adjustment row: L / W / H / distance / angle. Those figures are not decoration — change one and the model is redrawn and the verdict follows. The user does not have to measure precisely: the engine carries tolerance bands (rotated by ±10°, measured ±15%, unmeasured ±35–40% by category), and when the band is too wide it returns “suspected” rather than “confirmed”, together with which figure would settle it.

Fig. 14 — The same model, with the adjustment row showing

Tap the tree and a ruler rises from the bottom edge: L 8 m / W 8 m / H 8 m / D 30 m / angle 0° (the flat is on the 21st floor, eye level 62 m — an 8 m tree does not reach the sill, which is why it reads “nothing to settle”). Drag a slider or type a figure and the model above is redrawn at the new size.

The dimensions are the user’s input, not a fixed model.

The verdict card goes all the way: the object’s identity, the conclusion (“Even” — not a sha, keep it tidy), the reason (21 floors here, the block is 30 m, its roof sits about 32 m below the sill, so the pressing condition does not hold), and three expandable layers — floors, four other options, and the basis. It is not a one-word judgement, and the user is not asked to accept something they cannot adjust.

Fig. 15 — The verdict that follows from what was marked

The card states the object’s identity (Mao mountain, Zhen palace), the conclusion (“Even”: not a sha — keep it tidy), the reason (21 floors here, the block is 30 m, its roof sits about 32 m below the sill, so the “presses on you” condition does not hold), and three expandable layers: floors, other options (4), and why · basis.

Every conclusion carries its premise; change the premise and the conclusion changes.

8. The whole-house assessment: one line and one order

With indoors and outdoors both marked, the parts fold into a single assessment: 46 points, on the weak side (period: lower yuan, fire, 2024–2043), one line — “a few places where the air does not flow well, all within what can be adjusted; do these three first, do not start by thinking about moving” — and then three things that can be done without moving, each anchored to a specific palace and a specific action.

Fig. 16 — Whole-house assessment: nine palaces folded into one line

46 points · on the weak side (period: lower yuan, fire, 2024–2043), then one line — “a few places where the air does not flow well, all within what can be adjusted; do these three first, do not start by thinking about moving” — and a list of three things that can be done without moving: settle the sha in Li (due south) first, let the wealth corner in Xun (southeast) light up…

The system converges on one conclusion and one order of work, instead of handing over nine pages of text.

There is also a second path in this section, for how a person and a house go together: the birth time is entered and the app compares the house against that person. By the classical method people and houses each fall into an east group and a west group, and the two groups either match or they do not. When they do not, the method gives a set of adjustments rather than a verdict of “unsuitable” — which position to settle, which wall to leave free, which room to sleep in instead. What people often describe as “something felt off after we moved” is frequently not a bad house but one thing sitting in the wrong place; this section points at that one thing and gives the change in concrete terms.

Wording and limits (important): this app makes no promise about anyone’s health, lifespan, marriage or finances, and gives no medical, investment or legal advice. Every statement it produces is of the form “according to this written rule, from these inputs you entered”. The reading is reference material; what to do with it is the user’s decision. For anything to do with health, money or contracts, see a qualified professional.

9. The worksheet: ten pages a contractor can work from

The last step produces paper: “Build the checklist — 10 pages · printable”. One page of overall assessment, what to do for each direction, how to choose what to buy, and how to check the work afterwards. It is saved to Photos and sent to family or to the contractor. This is the app’s actual deliverable: the output leaves the app and lands in purchasing and construction.

Fig. 17 — The worksheet: ten pages that leave the phone

“Step 6 of 6 · Build the checklist, 10 pages · printable”: one page of overall assessment, what to do for each direction, what to buy, how to check the work afterwards. Generated, saved to Photos, sent to family or to the contractor.

The deliverable leaves the app — which is what makes it a tool rather than a content product.

The three pages below are from the real export in the English interface (pages 1, 8 and 10, exported at 1500×2120 and scaled here). They are not “more text inside the app”; they are a document that can be printed, handed to a contractor, and checked against three months later. The worksheet follows the interface language, so these pages read in English from the header down to the disclaimer in the footer.

Fig. 18 — Worksheet p.1: this house

The header carries the facts: sitting southeast, facing northwest, period-9 house (2024–2043), sitting 120° / facing 300°, Chen mountain. Each palace lists its mountain and facing stars and what has been marked in it; below that, a one-paragraph assessment, then the basis and how the facing was taken. The footer carries the disclaimer: layout reference only, not health or investment advice.

One page answers: what this house is, what it was computed from, and how far it can be used.

Fig. 19 — Worksheet p.8: buying and checking

One block per palace: what to buy (a tank 40–60 cm, water no deeper than 15 cm, six small fish; a bowl 10–15 cm across…), where to put it (against the southeast wall, 5–10 cm off it), and how to check it (a week later: water still clear, no scale, visible from the entrance). Each line has a box to tick and a space for the date.

This sheet is taken shopping and used for sign-off, not read once and forgotten.

Fig. 20 — Worksheet p.10: what to actually do

Ordered by sequence: the wealth corner in Xun (southeast) first — make it bright, then make it move, and do not get it wrong; then the four items in order — bed, stove, toilet, entrance. Each one is written as a checkable sentence (“headboard against a solid wall, not a window, not facing the door, not facing a mirror; no beam over the bed”), closing with the traditional-basis note.

Sequence and method are fixed on paper, so a contractor can work from it directly.

10. The source, and the limits we hold

  • Source: every verdict comes from Shen’s Xuan Kong Xue. The reading of each palace, the conditions under which each configuration holds, and the handling for each case all correspond to entries in that book. The system is not our invention, and we do not write “may” as if it were “will”.
  • What the app does not do: no card of the day, no randomly generated content, no social feed, no ads, no third-party analytics, no free-text chatbot. Every sentence on screen is computed from what the user entered.
  • Uncertain stays uncertain: an unmarked cell says “+ mark a function”, an unset facing says “Pending”, and a rough measurement is labelled “suspected” with a note on which figure would settle it.
  • Data stays on the device: charts, ledgers, the model and the worksheet all live on this phone. The cloud holds the account and, for subscribers, sync.

11. How it differs from other apps in this category

The descriptions below are taken from their published App Store listings at the time of writing. Their engines are their own and are not judged here — the comparison is only about how far each one carries the job:

What most listings in this category coverWhat this app does beyond that
A well-made compass: live 24 mountains, declination correction, overlay on a floor plan or a satellite map, tap a palace for a paragraph of star meaningsThe facing is only the first input: it selects the venue rule set, drives the chart, positions every object in the model and carries through to the printed page (Fig. 1–4)
One chart, one fixed paragraph per palace, written onceThe same chart feeds a measured 3D model and a screening pass over seven documented configurations; change a figure in metres and the verdict changes (Fig. 13–15)
LiDAR room scan, with the nine palaces laid over the scanned planNot a scan but a model built from metres: length, width, height, distance and rotation are all entered by the user, with the ruler right there (Fig. 13–14)
One photo in, one score out, with nothing showing how the score was reachedEvery verdict carries its premise, its tolerance and an expandable “why” (Fig. 15)
Indoor and outdoor conditions flattened into one listTwo ledgers that are never merged, each read on its own terms (Fig. 5–12)
A house assumed by default; an office or a shop gets the same wordingThree venue types, each with its own ledger and wording (Fig. 4, 8, 9)
The output is more text inside the app, or a screenshotThe output is a ten-page printable worksheet that can go straight to a contractor (Fig. 17–20)
A daily tip or a card of the dayNo daily content at all: every screen is computed from the two inputs

12. About this review

We understand what Guideline 4.3(b) is there to stop: bulk-reskinned apps with interchangeable content. This app is not that. It has no content library and no content feed; a user opens it because they have one specific building in hand. What it produces is not a readable passage but a model built in metres, a set of verdicts with explicit tolerances, and a document that goes to a site. If it would help, we can supply a full screen recording from facing to worksheet for any layout, or reproduce any input live during review.
